extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what factual findings and legal rationales are required to make a prima facie case of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 during patent examination, with illustrative examples and case law. Targets examiners and practitioners preparing or responding to obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear articulation / explicit analysis for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious. The analysis supporting a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 should be made explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must provide a reasoned explanation for every obviousness rejection; rejections cannot be sustained by mere conclusory statements. Courts (KSR; Ball Aerosol; In re Van Os) require that the examiner articulate the factual findings and explain how those findings support the legal conclusion of obviousness. Even when relying on common sense, Office personnel must articulate an appropriate rationale and factual basis (see MPEP §2141 and §2143).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To reject a claim based on this rationale, Office personnel must resolve the Graham factual inquiries and articulate the following findings: (1) that the prior art included each element claimed (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) that one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements as claimed by known methods and that in combination each element merely performs the same function as it does separately; (3) that one of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results of the combination were predictable; and (4) whatever additional findings based on the Graham factual inquiries are necessary. If any of these findings cannot be made, the combining-elements rationale cannot be used. Examples: Anderson’s-Black Rock, Sundance, Crocs (illustrating predictable results vs. unpredictability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prima facie case may be supported where substituting a known element for another would have produced predictable results to a person of ordinary skill. The examiner should explain why the substitution would have been made and why predictable results would follow, citing prior art and relevant factual findings. As with other rationales, findings must address Graham factors and any motivation to substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C: Use of known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products in the same way
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique to improve similar devices (methods, or products) in the same way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness may be supported when a known technique used in one apparatus or method would have been predictably applied to improve a similar apparatus or method. The examiner should articulate the similarity of devices/methods, the teaching of the technique, and the predictable nature of the improvement, with factual findings addressing the Graham inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D: Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement yields predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) ready for improvement to yield predictable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale supports rejection where the prior art shows a device primed for improvement and a known technique would predictably improve it. Examiner must show why the device was 'ready for improvement,' why the technique was known and applicable, and that predictable results would ensue. Provide factual findings and an articulated reason for combining the teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E: 'Obvious to try' — finite predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: "Obvious to try" — choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale supports obviousness when there are a limited number of predictable options and a person of ordinary skill would have had a reasonable expectation of success in trying them. Examiner must articulate the finite set of solutions, predictability, and expectation of success. Cases (e.g., Ecolab) emphasize that capability to optimize parameters and a reasonable expectation of success are material; if optimization is beyond ordinary skill or success is not reasonably expected, this rationale may not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F: Known work in one field prompts predictable variations for another field
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field of endeavor may prompt variations of it for use in either the same field or a different one based on design incentives or other market forces if the variations are predictable to one of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may rely on analogous techniques from another field where design incentives or market forces would have led one skilled in the art to adopt predictable variations. Must explain why the cross-field variation is predictable and pertinent to the problem. The scope of analogous art should be construed broadly when reasonably pertinent (see Wyers discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G: Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or to combine prior art reference teachings to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where prior art contains an express or implicit motivation to combine or modify references, examiner should identify that teaching/suggestion/motivation and explain how it would have led to the claimed combination. The MPEP notes the Federal Circuit guidance that motivation to combine need not always be an explicit teaching—reasonable inferences, common sense, or routine steps may supply the rationale—but the examiner must articulate the reasoning and factual basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any rationale must link factual findings to the legal conclusion of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Any rationale employed must provide a link between the factual findings and the legal conclusion of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must show how the resolved Graham inquiries (scope/content of prior art, differences between prior art and claims, level of ordinary skill, secondary considerations) support the chosen rationale and the ultimate legal conclusion. Mere conclusory statements that a combination would have been 'obvious' are insufficient; the examiner must articulate the inferences, reasoning, and factual underpinning (Ball Aerosol; KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability requirement and teaching away
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art teaches away from combining certain known elements, discovery of successful means of combining them is more likely to be nonobvious; combining known elements is insufficient if the results would not have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art discourages a combination or suggests incompatibility, an examiner should not rely on a combination-of-elements rationale unless they explain why the teaching away is overcome. Cases (Adams, Crocs) show that lack of predictability or teaching away can support nonobviousness. Examiners must analyze and state findings regarding any teachings in the prior art that would have discouraged the combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art: breadth and pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art references should be considered analogous if they are in the same field of endeavor or are reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed by the inventor; scope of analogous art is to be construed broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting combinations, examiner must explain why each reference is analogous or reasonably pertinent. The Wyers decision instructs that 'analogous art' may include references outside the immediate field if they are reasonably pertinent to solving the problem, and the MPEP directs examiners to articulate that reasoning. Analogous-art analysis is part of the factual Graham inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of the capabilities of a person of ordinary skill (expectation of success and ability to optimize)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting obviousness based on modifying or combining prior art, assess whether optimization or parameter-adjustment would have been within the level of ordinary skill and whether a reasonable expectation of success existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecolab and related cases indicate that if one skilled in the art would know how to adjust parameters and would reasonably expect success, then obviousness is supported; if optimization is beyond ordinary skill or the expectation of success is absent, obviousness may not be appropriate. Examiner should make explicit findings about the skill level and the expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claim limitations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: All claim limitations must be considered in assessing obviousness; one cannot ignore claim limitations when forming a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner must analyze every claimed limitation and explain how the prior art teaches or renders obvious each limitation (or why inherent/implicit disclosure applies). Failure to consider any limitation may render the rejection unsupported. See MPEP §2143 heading and related discussions.
